summary: Specifies changes to the Policy Core Information Model from RFC 3060. It introduces entirely new elements, such as classes for header filtering, and deprecates some existing ones, such as policy rule priorities, replacing them with better alternatives.

eli5.summary: Policy models describe rules like who gets what network service. This note fixes and extends the original rule-describing model, adding new pieces and swapping out weak ones.

subtitle: Extensions to the Policy Core Information Model: reusable and nested rules, decision strategies, variables and values, and packet filters.

tldr.problem: The original Policy Core Information Model (PCIM, RFC 3060) had gaps: a confusingly named repository class, priorities attached to rules, no way to assign roles to resources, and no shared way to express packet filters.
tldr.mechanism: PCIMe adds new classes (policy sets, compound and simple conditions and actions, variables and values, packet filter classes) and deprecates others, each deprecation naming its replacement, in ways that keep interoperability with PCIM where possible.
tldr.outcome: Submodels such as QoS and IPsec policy models can build on a richer core. The RFC updates RFC 3060 and says the extensions add no new security considerations.

today: RFC 3460 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3060. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What PCIMe Changes
sections.content:
RFC 3460, known as PCIMe, specifies changes to the Policy Core Information Model in RFC 3060. It makes two kinds of change. Some elements are entirely new, such as classes for header filtering. Others, such as policy rule priorities, are deprecated and replaced. Both are done so that, as far as possible, implementations of the original model still interoperate.

The RFC borrows the change rules of the CIM model: properties can be added to classes, classes and properties can be marked DEPRECATED (with a named replacement, or "No value"), classes can be inserted above existing ones with properties pulled up, and new subclasses can be defined below existing ones.

The eight headline changes are: replace PolicyRepository; clarify how rules and groups are aggregated; change how rule priority is represented and add decision strategies; expand policy roles; add compound conditions and actions; add variables and values; add variable and value subclasses for packet-header filtering; and add classes for device-level packet filtering.
sections.eli5: The first rulebook worked but had missing pages and a few badly labeled ones. This document adds the missing pages and relabels the confusing ones, crossing out the old labels so you know what replaced them.

sections.title: Reusable and Nested Policy Structure
sections.content:
PCIM's PolicyRepository class shares its name with the Policy Repository in the Policy Framework, where the PDP retrieves policy. To avoid that confusion it is deprecated in favor of ReusablePolicyContainer. A single association, ReusablePolicy, now lets any policy element be placed in such a container, not just conditions and actions.

A new abstract class PolicySet sits above PolicyGroup and PolicyRule. It carries the PolicyDecisionStrategy and PolicyRoles properties. The aggregation PolicySetComponent replaces two PCIM aggregations and lets groups and rules nest in either direction. Loops, including a set that contains itself, are not allowed.

Nested rules follow set rules. The parent's conditions are ANDed with the sub-rules' conditions. If the parent's conditions are true, its actions run before the sub-rules' actions. A default action must be modeled as a catchall sub-rule with the lowest priority. That acts as a default under FirstMatching, but under AllMatching it is always performed.
sections.eli5: Rules can now sit inside other rules, like a folder inside a folder. The outer rule has to be true first, and a final catch-all rule can say what to do if nothing else fit.

sections.title: Priorities and Decision Strategies
sections.content:
A decision strategy says how the rules in a PolicySet are evaluated. FirstMatching enforces only the actions of the highest-priority rule whose conditions are true. AllMatching enforces the actions of every rule that matches. Implementations MUST support FirstMatching and MAY support AllMatching. The default is FirstMatching.

Priority moves off the rule. PolicyRule.Priority is deprecated, and priority now lives on the PolicySetComponent aggregation, so it only matters relative to its siblings. The larger value is the higher priority, and the value MUST be unique within the aggregating PolicySet. Disjoint ("unrooted") sets that apply to the same resource and functional domain are combined with FirstMatching, using the priority on PolicySetInSystem.

Under AllMatching, higher-priority actions run first, so a lower-priority rule can have the "last word". The RFC's example: one rule sets the DSCP to 3 and a lower-priority rule sets it to 4, so 4 wins. Side effects of evaluating conditions or running actions MUST NOT affect other conditions in the same evaluation pass.
sections.eli5: When more than one rule fits, you can pick the first one only, or do them all in order. Each rule gets a rank number so there is never a tie.

sections.title: Policy Roles
sections.content:
A policy role is a label on a managed element, such as an interface, that selects which rules apply to it. PCIMe moves PolicyRoles up to PolicySet so groups as well as rules can carry roles, and nested rules and groups implicitly inherit the roles of their container. There is no copying, so inconsistent roles are possible, and handling them is beyond the scope of PCIMe.

PCIM had no formal way to say which resources have a role. The new PolicyRoleCollection class fills the gap: resources are aggregated into it through ElementInPolicyRoleCollection, and its PolicyRole property holds the role name. The RFC's example is 20 traffic trunks, three of which get "Gold Service" by being placed in a collection with that role, so a PDP knows which rules apply to them.

Roles are used to optimize policy retrieval. Implementing them is not mandatory, but if they are used, either the collection approach or elements reporting their pre-programmed roles (as in COPS) should be supported.
sections.eli5: A role is a sticker such as "Gold Service". Stick it on the rules and on the things they apply to, and everyone knows which rules go with which things.

sections.title: Compound, Simple, Variables and Values
sections.content:
A CompoundPolicyCondition is a Boolean combination (DNF or CNF) of simpler conditions, and a CompoundPolicyAction is a sequence of actions treated as one logical action, such as "shape and mark". Both can be stored as reusable pieces. A new ExecutionStrategy property, on PolicyRule and CompoundPolicyAction, takes the values Do Until Success, Do All (the default) and Do Until Failure.

A SimplePolicyCondition is a pair, variable MATCH value, and a SimplePolicyAction means "set variable to value". The MATCH operator is implied and depends on the variable and value types. Generic rules cover singletons, ranges and sets; for example a range matches a range if all its values fall inside the other. If the types differ, the condition is false. A set operation overwrites the old value completely.

Variables come in two kinds. Explicit variables name a model class and property (ModelClass, ModelProperty) and are bound to instances chosen by policy roles. Implicit variables, such as source port, describe things that are not modeled as objects, like packets. They are modeled as subclasses so submodels can add more without a shared enumeration. Values come as strings, integers, bit strings, Booleans, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and MAC addresses.

The ExpectedPolicyValuesForVariable association exists for validation before deployment. It plays no role in deciding whether a condition is true, or in running an action.
sections.eli5: A simple rule is a question like "is the port 80?" Fancy rules combine questions with and, or and not. Actions can be bundled too, like doing two chores in a set order.

sections.title: Packet Filtering Classes
sections.content:
PCIMe gives two ways to express packet filters. The domain-level model builds a CompoundFilterCondition from SimplePolicyCondition instances, one per header field, using predefined variables for IP and common layer 2 fields plus a flow-direction variable. Its IsMirrored property makes one filter match traffic in both directions by flipping source and destination fields, including direction, addresses, ports, MAC addresses and SAPs.

The device-level model uses subclasses of FilterEntryBase: IpHeadersFilter for IP, TCP and UDP headers and 8021Filter for 802 MAC headers. One instance can describe many fields, and values are stored in native form rather than as strings. Entries are never used alone. They are aggregated into a FilterList, whose entries are ANDed because EntrySequence is always 0. The list's Direction property can be Input, Output, Both or Mirrored.

In IpHeadersFilter, a property that is absent matches all values. HdrIpVersion is 4 or 6, and decides the size of the address fields. PCIMe provides no mapping between the two levels.
sections.eli5: A filter is a checklist for mail, such as "from this street, going to that street". There is a simple checklist version and a detailed all-in-one form. A mirror setting lets the same checklist work for mail coming back the other way.

sections.title: Conformance and Security
sections.content:
PCIM and PCIMe define elements that submodels may use and say nothing about whether implementations must support them. A submodel SHOULD state which elements its implementations must, should or may support, and stay silent on the ones it does not use. The behavior of undefined or incorrectly defined conditions and actions is not prescribed.

On security, the RFC refers to the general considerations in PCIM (RFC 3060) and says the extensions add no additional considerations.
sections.eli5: This document only provides the building blocks. Whoever builds with them decides what must be supported. It adds no new safety worries beyond the first rulebook.

items.label: Do Until Success
items.desc: Execute actions in the predefined order until a single action succeeds.

items.label: Do All
items.desc: Execute all actions in order, even if one or more fail. This is the default.

items.label: Do Until Failure
items.desc: Execute actions in order until the first failure.
